title: Hansen Site (15GP14)
summary: In Greenup County, the Hansen Site holds Late Archaic summer camps and later Woodland and Fort Ancient communities spread over thousands of years.
bodyMarkdown:
The Hansen Site (15Gp14) is an archaeological site in Greenup County. It covers about 15 acres (6 hectares). Native people returned to this spot again and again over thousands of years, and their camps and houses left a layered record that archaeologists have studied.

An account of [the Hansen Site](https://grokipedia.com/page/hansen_site) counts it among several important archaeological sites in Greenup County.

## Late Archaic summer camps

The earliest known use of the site dates to the Late Archaic period, around 2000 BCE. Archaeologists think people lived there lightly, probably during the summer months. They left distinctive projectile points, among them the Merom and Rowlette styles. Tests of material from the excavations returned uncalibrated dates of 2060 and 1930 BCE.

## Two Woodland villages

People came back during the Middle and Late Woodland periods, in two separate episodes. The first, from about 300 to 450 CE, was an intensive occupation centered on three circular buildings made with single posts, along with small clusters of households. Excavators found evidence of stone tool making, food storage and waste disposal.

The second episode, from about 500 to 600 CE, looked different. Life centered on more communal structures, and work such as tool making seems to have taken place in shared areas.

## Earthworks of the same era

The Hansen article says that during this time, Adena people in Greenup County built earthworks in the county. Other accounts credit the region's large earthworks to the Adena and Ohio Hopewell cultures between 100 BCE and 500 CE, which would place most of the building before Hansen's second village. Readers should treat the exact timing as unsettled.

## Later visitors

The Hansen article says Fort Ancient people used the site after 600 CE. An account of [the Fort Ancient culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient) dates that culture to about 1000–1750 CE. Both dates are shown here because the sources do not agree.

Centuries later, Shawnee, Iroquois and Delaware people made the Ohio Valley a center of trade and diplomacy.

## Kentucky today

Most of what is known about the Hansen Site comes from chapters by Richard W. Jeffries and Darlene Applegate in The Archaeology of Kentucky: An Update, published by the Kentucky Heritage Council in 2008. The site is a record of Native life in Greenup County across thousands of years. Its buried remains are best left undisturbed.
